questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

Replace “bidden” with “bid”.

Rule / Concept: Forms of the Verb 'Bid'

The verb Bid is a classic trap because it follows two entirely different sets of inflections based on its meaning:

Meaning: To offer a price (Auction/Tender)

V1: Bid V2: Bid V3: Bid

Meaning: To wish, command, or say goodbye (Farewell/Order)

V1: Bid V2: Bade V3: Bidden

💢 Application to the Given Question - In this sentence, the context is an auction (offering money for a portrait). When "bid" is used in the context of money or auctions, its Past Tense (V2) is simply bid. The word "bidden" is the Past Participle (V3) used only for commands or wishes (e.g., "He was bidden to come"). Using "bidden" in an auction context is a grammatical error.

More Examples for Clarity -

Example 1 ✅: He bid 10,000 rupees for the antique watch yesterday. (Auction – V2)

Example 2 ✅: She bade him goodnight before leaving. (Wish - V2)

Example 3 ✅: I have bidden him to stay away from trouble. (Command - V3)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) - “does it”.

📌 Rule / Concept: “Nothing” as Negative Subject + Do-Support

Words like nothing, nobody, no one, none make a sentence negative in meaning.

When the statement is negative → the question tag must be positive.

Also, when the main clause does not contain an auxiliary verb (like is/was/has/had), we use do-support according to tense.

💢 Application to the Given Question

  • “Nothing” → negative meaning

  • Therefore → tag must be positive

  • Main verb = suggests (simple present)

  • No auxiliary present → use does

  • “Nothing” refers to a thing → pronoun = it

So the correct tag is: does it?

✅ More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ - Nothing was discussed during the meeting, was it?

Example 2 ✅ - Nothing has changed so far, has it?

Example 3 ✅ - Nothing seems unusual, does it?

🧠 Things to Remember

  • Nothing = negative meaning

  • Negative meaning → positive tag

  • Use do-support if no auxiliary is present

  • Use “it” for non-person reference

options_en: The inflation rate over the past few months has been
growing more and more severe, making it difficult
for common people to manage household expenses.
No error.
options_hi: The inflation rate over the past few months has been
growing more and more severe, making it difficult
for common people to manage household expenses.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) – replace “more and more severe” with “worse and worse”.

Rule/Concept: Graduation of Comparison (Double Comparison Logic):

When a quality increases continuously, use the structure: Comparative + and + Comparative.

Do not use “more and more + adjective” with a positive form (e.g., “more and more severe”) when a comparative form exists.

Corrected Sentence -

The inflation rate over the past few months has been growing worse and worse, making it difficult for common people to manage household expenses.

More Examples for Clarity -

The weather is getting hotter and hotter as summer progresses.

The students’ anxiety about exams is becoming greater and greater each day.

Traffic congestion in the city is becoming worse and worse despite new measures.

Incorrect Usage -

The situation is becoming more and more bad.

The workload is getting more and more heavy.

questions.solution_en:
Replace “can be able to” with “will be able to” or “can”.

Rule / Concept: Redundancy of Ability –

In English grammar, the modal verb 'Can' itself denotes power, ability, or capacity. Similarly, the phrase 'Be able to' also denotes ability. Using both together in a single clause creates a redundancy, which is grammatically incorrect. To express future ability, we use "will be able to," and for present ability, we use "can."

Application to the Given Question - In the provided sentence, the use of "can" along with "be able to" is redundant because both terms serve the same purpose of expressing ability. Since the sentence refers to a future goal (executing the migration before the fiscal year ends), "will be able to" is the most appropriate correction.

More Examples for Clarity

  1. I can solve this high-level puzzle within minutes. ✔

  2. We cannot be able to finish the project by Friday. ✘

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  1. The "Can/Able" Trap: If you see 'can' and 'able' in the same part of the sentence, it is 99% likely to be the error.

  2. Tense Check: Use 'Can' for present ability, 'Could' for past ability, and 'Will be able to' for future ability.

  3. Contextual Logic: Sometimes 'can' is replaced by 'will be able to' to maintain the logical flow of a sentence referring to a future possibility.

balance, many successful entrepreneurs avoid
to check their emails after midnight.
No Error
options_hi: In order to maintain a healthy work-life
balance, many successful entrepreneurs avoid
to check their emails after midnight.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “to check” with “checking”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Verbs followed by Gerunds

n English, certain verbs are transitively followed by a Gerund (V{ing}) rather than an Infinitive (to + V1). The verb "Avoid" is a prime example. When we use "avoid," the action that follows must be in the noun-form (Gerund) to complete the meaning of the sentence. Using an infinitive after "avoid" is grammatically incorrect in formal English.

💢 Application to the Given Question

"...many successful entrepreneurs avoid to check their emails..."

In this sentence, the verb "avoid" is the main action. The secondary action, which is the act of checking emails, must be expressed as a Gerund. Therefore, the infinitive "to check" must be changed to the gerund "checking" to satisfy the grammatical requirement of the verb "avoid."

Corrected Sentence

In order to maintain a healthy work-life balance, many successful entrepreneurs avoid checking their emails after midnight.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅ You should avoid making hasty decisions during a crisis.

Example 2 ✅ Most people detest waiting in long queues at the billing counter.

Example 3 ✅ The committee suggested implementing the new policy immediately.

REMEMBAER THE LIST

Verbs that are followed by gerund:- detest, mind, resent, avoid, Stop, excuse, resist, miss, prevent, defer, delay, postpone, consider, risk

appreciate, admire, forget, forgive, recollect, remember, suggest, etc

📌 Rule / Concept: Second Conditional (Inversion with "Were")

The Second Conditional is used to describe an imaginary or hypothetical present situation. When we use "Were" at the beginning of a sentence (Inversion), it replaces "If + Subject + were".

The structure must be: Were + Subject + ..., Subject + would/could/might + V1(Infinitive).

💢 Application to the Given Question - The sentence starts with "Were the CEO... aware," which establishes a hypothetical present state (the CEO is currently not aware). According to the rules of the Second Conditional, the result clause must use "would + V1". The original sentence incorrectly uses "would have taken" (V3), which is the structure for a past hypothetical (Third Conditional).

More Examples for Clarity

Example 2 ✅: Were she taller, she could become a professional model.

Example 3 ✅: Were they to lose the contract, the company would struggle to survive.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

📌 Rule / Concept: Present Continuous (Phrasal Verb) – Active to Passive Conversion

In the Present Continuous tense, the active structure is: Subject + is/am/are + V¹+ing + Object. The passive structure becomes: Object + is/am/are + being + V³ (+ by + Subject). When the verb is a phrasal verb (e.g., look into), the preposition must be retained in passive form, and the tense must remain unchanged.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The liquidators are looking into the discrepancy between the reported assets and the physical inventory. Here, “are looking into” is in the present continuous tense. “The discrepancy between the reported assets and the physical inventory” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since it is singular, the correct auxiliary is “is.” The correct passive structure is: is + being + looked into. Option (A) is incorrect because it omits the preposition “into.” Option (B) incorrectly changes the tense to past continuous. Option (D) shifts the tense to present perfect.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

For continuous tenses, always use “being” in passive voice. Never drop the preposition in phrasal verbs. Maintain the original tense. Ensure subject–verb agreement with the new subject.
questions.solution_hi:
The Correct Ans is Option (C)

📌 Rule / Concept: Present Continuous (Phrasal Verb) – Active to Passive Conversion

In the Present Continuous tense, the active structure is: Subject + is/am/are + V¹+ing + Object. The passive structure becomes: Object + is/am/are + being + V³ (+ by + Subject). When the verb is a phrasal verb (e.g., look into), the preposition must be retained in passive form, and the tense must remain unchanged.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The liquidators are looking into the discrepancy between the reported assets and the physical inventory. Here, “are looking into” is in the present continuous tense. “The discrepancy between the reported assets and the physical inventory” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since it is singular, the correct auxiliary is “is.” The correct passive structure is: is + being + looked into. Option (A) is incorrect because it omits the preposition “into.” Option (B) incorrectly changes the tense to past continuous. Option (D) shifts the tense to present perfect.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

For continuous tenses, always use “being” in passive voice. Never drop the preposition in phrasal verbs. Maintain the original tense. Ensure subject–verb agreement with the new subject.

📌 Rule / Concept: Gerund after Verb (“Resent”) – Passive Gerund Formation

Certain verbs like resent, avoid, enjoy, deny, appreciate are followed by a gerund (V-ing). When converting such structures into passive, the correct form is: Subject + resent + being + V³. The structure “to be + V³” is incorrect after verbs that require a gerund. The tense must remain unchanged.

📌 Application to the Given Question

The junior analysts resent the manager giving them menial data-entry tasks. Here, “resent” is followed by a gerund clause (“the manager giving…”). In passive reconstruction, the correct form is “resent being given…” since “resent” takes a gerund, not an infinitive. Hence, “The junior analysts resent being given menial data-entry tasks by the manager” is correct. Option (B) incorrectly uses the infinitive (“to be given”). Option (C) distorts the structure. Option (D) incorrectly changes the tense and construction.

💡 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

After verbs like resent, avoid, enjoy, use a gerund (V-ing). In passive gerund form, use “being + V³.” Do not use the infinitive (“to be”) after such verbs. Maintain the original tense carefully.

Rule / Concept: Reciprocal Pronouns (Each other vs. One another)

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (A).

Replace “an advice” with “advice” or “a piece of advice”.

Rule / Concept: Uncountable Nouns (Advice) -

In English grammar, "Advice" is an uncountable noun. This means it cannot be counted as one, two, or three. Because it is uncountable:

-It does not have a plural form ("advices" is incorrect).

-It cannot be preceded by the indefinite article 'a' or 'an'.

-To express a singular quantity, we must use a countable phrase like "a piece of" or "a word of"

Corrected Sentence - She sought advice (or a piece of advice) from her mentor before deciding to resign from her lucrative position at the firm.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips -

-The Plurality Trick: If the sentence implies multiple suggestions, use "many pieces of advice" or "some advice," but never "advices."

-Confusing Pair: Do not confuse the noun Advice (ending in -ice) with the verb Advise (ending in -ise). You give advice (noun), but you advise someone (verb).

questions.solution_en:
Rule/Concept: Would Rather (Preference)

The phrase "would rather" is a fixed idiomatic expression used to denote a preference. It is always followed by the base form of the verb (V1). In competitive exams, this is a frequent "fixed pair" trap where examiners replace 'would' with 'could', 'should', or 'will' to test the student's familiarity with standard English usage.

Application to the Given Question - The sentence expresses a strong preference of the committee (choosing suspension over compromising sovereignty). The presence of the word "rather" acts as a definitive keyword that necessitates the use of "would".

More Examples for Clarity-

  1. I would rather stay at home than go to the party.

  2. She would rather resign than apologize for something she didn't do.

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

  1. The "Rather" Trigger: Whenever you see 'rather' followed by a 'than' later in the sentence, your mind should immediately look for "would".

  2. V1 check: Ensure no "to" is placed after "would rather." It is always Would rather + V1.

  3. Negative Form: The negative is "would rather not" (e.g., I would rather not go).

📌 Rule / Concept: Redundant Object Pronouns in Relative Clauses -

In a relative clause, the relative pronoun (who, whom, which, that) acts as the object or subject of the verb within that clause. If the relative pronoun already represents the object, adding a personal pronoun (like him, her, it, them) to serve as that same object creates a grammatical redundancy called a "double object."

KEY RULE: NO OF SUBJECT=NO OF VERB (Always check )

Application to the Given Question

"had tracked him across several international borders"

In this sentence, "whom" is the relative pronoun acting as the object of the verb "tracked." By including the pronoun "him," the sentence effectively provides two objects for the same verb. To correct this, the redundant pronoun "him" must be removed.

Corrected Sentence - The high-profile fugitive, whom the special forces had tracked across several international borders, was finally apprehended at a remote safehouse.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 : The expensive car, which my father bought last year, has already broken down. ✅

Example 2 : This is the candidate whom the committee selected for the prestigious role ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1 : The expensive car, which my father bought it last year, has already broken down. ❌

Wrong example 2 : This is the candidate whom the committee selected him for the role. ❌

questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Only with this specialized diagnostic tool, the technicians can identify
the minute structural defects within the turbine's internal
components before they lead to a catastrophic mechanical failure.
No Error
options_hi: Only with this specialized diagnostic tool, the technicians can identify
the minute structural defects within the turbine's internal
components before they lead to a catastrophic mechanical failure.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A)

Replace “the technicians can” with “can the technicians”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Inversion with "Only + Prepositional Phrase / Adverbial"

When a sentence begins with "Only" followed by a prepositional phrase (e.g., Only with..., Only by..., Only in...) or an adverbial clause (e.g., Only when..., Only after...), the main clause must undergo Inversion. The auxiliary verb (can, could, do, does, did, have, has) must be placed before the subject.

If senetence starts with Only + time / Adverb of manner, use inversion.

Eg. :- Only yesterday, Only then, Only after a month,

Only the day before yesterday, Only after a year, Only in this way,

Only by working hard, etc.

💢 Application to the Given Question

Only with this specialized diagnostic tool, the technicians can identify...

In this sentence, the restrictive phrase "Only with this specialized diagnostic tool" is placed at the very beginning to emphasize the condition. According to the rule of inversion, the auxiliary verb "can" must move to the position before the subject "the technicians" to maintain the correct grammatical structure of the sentence.

Corrected Sentence

Only with this specialized diagnostic tool can the technicians identify the minute structural defects within the turbine's internal components before they lead to a catastrophic mechanical failure.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1 ✅: Only by working hard can you achieve success in the SSC CGL exam.

Example 2 ✅: Only after the storm subsided did we venture outside to check the damage.

Example 3 ✅: Only in this small village can such rare artifacts be found.

🧠 Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • The "Only" Trap: Remember that inversion doesn't happen if "Only" modifies the subject directly (e.g., "Only the technicians can identify the error" is correct and requires no inversion).

  • Identify the Phrase: Look for a preposition (with, by, in) or a conjunction (when, after) immediately following "Only".

  • The Main Clause: In complex sentences starting with Only when or Only after, the inversion happens in the main clause, not the subordinate clause.
